name: Sulayman ibn Mihran al-A'mash
nameAr: سليمان بن مِهران الأسدي الكاهلي مولاهم الكوفي، الأعمش

laqab.en: al-A'mash, the weak-sighted; he is cited by this name far more often than by his own

nisbas.en: al-Asadi al-Kahili (as a client of Banu Kahil of Asad)

mawla: Banu Kahil, a branch of Asad

orthography.spelled: Mihran: with a kasra on the mim (مِهران).
orthography.source: Hammad al-Ansari's summary of Tabaqat al-Mudallisin (Shamela 22949/12)

bornNote: Born at the beginning of 61 AH, the day al-Husayn was killed (Taqrib; al-Ijli); Ibn Hibban puts his birth two years earlier

deathVariants.authority: Waki' and others; preferred by al-Khatib

taqrib.ar: ثقة حافظ عارف بالقراءات، ورع، لكنه يدلس
taqrib.en: Reliable, a hadith master, expert in the Qur'anic readings, scrupulous; but he uses the ambiguous formula.

role: The hadith scholar and Qur'an reciter of Kufa in his generation

teachers.name: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i
teachers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1597; Sahih Muslim 1270; Sunan Abi Dawud 1873; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 860; Sunan al-Nasa'i 2937

teachers.name: Qays ibn Abi Hazim
teachers.source: reciprocal of the entry in qays-ibn-abi-hazim's record (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib)

students.name: Yahya al-Qattan
students.source: reciprocal of the entry in yahya-ibn-said-al-qattan's record (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib)

verdicts.ar: أجود الأسانيد: الأعمش عن إبراهيم عن علقمة عن عبد الله
verdicts.en: The finest of chains: al-A'mash from Ibrahim from Alqama from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Asked whether al-A'mash was like al-Zuhri, he refused the comparison in al-A'mash's favour: al-Zuhri accepted reading-back and licence and worked for the Umayyads, while al-A'mash was poor, patient, kept away from rulers, scrupulous and learned in the Qur'an.

verdicts.critic: Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Ammar al-Mawsili
verdicts.ar: ليس في المحدثين أثبت من الأعمش، ومنصور بن المعتمر وهو ثبت أيضا
verdicts.en: There is no one among the hadith scholars firmer than al-A'mash; Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir is also firm, but al-A'mash knows the connected reports better and has more of them.

verdicts.ar: كان ثقة ثبتا في الحديث، وكان محدث أهل الكوفة في زمانه، ولم يكن له كتاب، وكان رأسا في القرآن
verdicts.en: He was reliable and firm in hadith, the hadith scholar of the Kufans in his time; he had no written book, and he was a leading authority in the Qur'an.

verdicts.ar: سبق الأعمش أصحابه بأربع: كان أقرأهم للقرآن، وأحفظهم للحديث، وأعلمهم بالفرائض
verdicts.en: Al-A'mash outstripped his companions in four things: he was the best reciter of the Qur'an among them, the best in memory for hadith, the most learned in inheritance law, and a fourth he mentioned.

verdicts.ar: دلس عن زيد بن وهب كثيرا، وعن أبي الضحى وإبراهيم بن يزيد وأبي صالح ومجاهد وشقيق
verdicts.en: He used the ambiguous formula a great deal over Zayd ibn Wahb, and over Abu al-Duha, Ibrahim ibn Yazid, Abu Salih, Mujahid and Shaqiq.
verdicts.source: Ibn Hajar, Ta'rif Ahl al-Taqdis, as quoted on the Shamela narrator record (1/118)

dhahabi.en: The hadith master, one of the leading authorities.

tadlis.source: Ibn Hajar, Ta'rif Ahl al-Taqdis (Tabaqat al-Mudallisin), entry 55, second rank: described as a mudallis by al-Karabisi, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni
tadlis.note: Al-Dhahabi's rule, quoted in Hammad al-Ansari's summary of the Tabaqat: when al-A'mash says 'he narrated to us' there is no question; when he says 'from', tadlis is possible, except from the teachers he narrated from abundantly, such as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Abu Wa'il and Abu Salih al-Samman, whose reports are treated as connected. Here he says 'from Ibrahim', one of exactly those teachers. The class notes add that Musnad Ahmad has al-A'mash saying 'Ibrahim narrated to us' for this hadith; that route was not checked for this record.

bio: The leading hadith scholar and Qur'an reciter of Kufa between the generation of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, his teacher, and that of Sufyan al-Thawri and Shu'ba, his students. Born the year al-Husayn was killed, he taught for half a century without a written book and died in 148 AH. He was known by his nickname, the weak-sighted, so completely that his real name, Sulayman ibn Mihran, can go unrecognised. The one reservation the critics record is his use of the ambiguous formula, and they also record the rule for handling it.
